slots.text:
… Ich, roh geprägt, und aller Reize baar.
Vor leicht sich dreh'nden Nymphen mich zu brüsten;
Ich, so verkürzt um schönes Ebenmass,
Geschändet von der tückischen Natur,
Entstellt, verwahrlost, vor der Zeit gesandt
In diese Welt des Athmens, halb kaum fertig
Gemacht, und zwar so lahm und ungeziemend,
Dass Hunde bellen, hink' ich wo vorbei.
[… I, that am rudely stamp’d, and want love’s majesty / To strut before a wanton ambling nymph; / I, that am curtail’d of this fair proportion, / Cheated of feature by dissembling nature, / Deform’d, unfinish’d, sent before my time / Into this breathing world, scarce half made up, / And that so lamely and unfashionable / That dogs bark at me as I halt by them.]

Natures such as Gloucester’s cannot be saved by being mediated into an idea of society. Ethics really only makes fools of them — much as ethics would be mocking Sarah if it asked her: “Why don’t you express the universal and marry?” Such natures are in the paradox from the very ground up. They are by no means less perfect than other people; only, they are either lost in the demonic paradox or saved in the divine one. Now, time and again people have taken pleasure in the fact that witches, goblins, trolls and so on were misshapen creatures; and it is undeniable that every human being has an inclination, on seeing a misshapen creature, at once to attach to it the notion of a moral depravity. What a monstrous injustice! For the relation must rather be turned around: existence itself has corrupted them, the way a stepmother makes children turn out badly. To be placed outside the universal from the start, by nature or by historical circumstance — that is the beginning of the demonic, for which the individual himself, however, bears no guilt. In this way Cumberland’s Jew, too, is a demon, even though he does good. In this way the demonic can also show itself as contempt for people — a contempt, note carefully, that does not lead the demonic person himself to act contemptibly. On the contrary, his strength lies in knowing that he is better than all those who judge him. — About all such things the poet, of all people, ought to be the first to raise the alarm. God knows what books the younger versifiers now living read! Their study probably consists in learning rhymes by heart. God knows what their significance in existence is! At this moment I do not know that they are of any use except that they furnish an edifying proof of the immortality of the soul: one can confidently say of them to oneself what Baggesen says of the town poet Kildevalle — “if he becomes immortal, then we all will.” — What has been said here on the occasion of Sarah was said chiefly with a view to poetic production, and therefore on a fanciful presupposition. But it has its full significance if one wanted, with psychological interest, to go deeply into the meaning of the old saying: nullum unquam exstitit magnum ingenium sine aliqua dementia — there has never been a great genius without some touch of madness. For this dementia is the genius’s suffering in existence. It is the expression of — if I dare say so — the divine envy, while the genius in him is the expression of the divine partiality. So from the beginning the genius is disoriented in relation to the universal and brought into relation with the paradox. This holds whether, in despair over his limit — which in his eyes turns his omnipotence into impotence — he seeks a demonic reassurance, and therefore will not admit this, either before God or before people, or whether he reassures himself religiously in love for the deity. Here lie psychological tasks to which, it seems to me, one could gladly sacrifice a whole life; and yet a word about them is so rarely heard. What relation does madness bear to genius? Can the one be constructed out of the other? In what sense, and to what extent, is the genius in command of his madness? For it is obvious that up to a point he is in command of it — otherwise he really would be mad. For such observations, however, ingenuity is required in a high degree, and love as well; for to observe someone superior is very difficult. If one were to read through some of the most brilliant authors with attention to this, it might perhaps be possible, once in a great while and with much effort, to discover a little.

I will imagine one more case: an individual who wants to save the universal by being concealed and by his silence. I can use the legend of Faust for this. Faust is a doubter, an apostate of the spirit who goes the way of the flesh. That is the poets’ view of him. And while it is said again and again that every age has its Faust, the age’s poets nonetheless go, one after another, undaunted down the same beaten track. Let us make a small change. Faust is the doubter κατ’ ἐξοχήν — the doubter above all others; but he is a sympathetic nature. Even in Goethe’s conception of Faust I miss a deeper psychological insight into doubt’s secret conversations with itself. In our time, when after all everyone has experienced doubt, no poet has yet taken a single step in that direction. So I think I could well offer them royal bonds to write on, so that they could write down all the many things they have experienced in this respect — they would hardly fill more than the margin on the front.

notes.text: If one does not want to use a doubter, one could choose a similar figure — an ironist, for example, whose sharp eye has seen to the bottom of the ridiculousness of existence, and whom a secret understanding with the forces of life assures of what the patient wishes. He knows that he has the power of laughter if he wants to use it; he is sure of his victory — indeed, what is more, of his good fortune. He knows that a single voice will be raised to hold him back, but he knows that he is stronger. He knows that one can still, for a moment, get the men to look serious, but he also knows that in secret they long to laugh with him. He knows that one can still, for a moment, get the woman to hold her fan before her eyes when he speaks; but he knows she is laughing behind the fan; he knows the fan is not absolutely opaque; he knows one can write invisible writing on it; he knows that whenever a woman strikes at him with her fan, that is because she has understood him. He knows unerringly how laughter steals into a person and lives there hidden, and how, once it has taken up lodging, it sits lying in wait. Let us picture such an Aristophanes, such a Voltaire, slightly altered: for he is also a sympathetic nature. He loves existence, he loves people, and he knows that even if laughter’s condemnation may perhaps bring up a young generation that is saved, a great many people in the present generation will go under. So he keeps silent, and as far as possible forgets to laugh himself. But dare he keep silent? Perhaps there are quite a few who do not understand at all the difficulty I am speaking of. They probably think it was an admirable magnanimity to keep silent. That is not at all my view. For I think that any such nature, if he has not had the magnanimity to keep silent, is a traitor to existence. So I demand this magnanimity of him; but when he has it, dare he then keep silent? Ethics is a dangerous science, and it may well be that Aristophanes, determined on purely ethical grounds, resolved to let laughter pass judgment on the age that had gone astray. Aesthetic magnanimity cannot help here; for one does not venture such things on the strength of that. If he is to keep silent, he must go into the paradox. — I will hint at one more design: that a person, for example, possesses an explanation of a hero’s life that explains it in a lamentable way, and yet a whole contemporary age rests absolutely secure in this hero without suspecting anything of the kind.

slots.text: Only when Faust is bent back into himself in this way — only then can doubt look poetic; only then, too, does he himself actually discover all its sufferings in actuality. He knows, then, that it is spirit that sustains existence. But he also knows that the security and joy in which people live are not grounded in the power of spirit, but are easily explained as an unreflective bliss. As a doubter — as the doubter — he is higher than all of this. And if anyone tries to deceive him by claiming to have gone through doubt himself, Faust easily sees through it. For whoever has made a movement in the world of spirit — that is, an infinite movement — can tell at once, just by listening to what someone says, whether the one speaking is a tried man or a Münchhausen. What a Tamerlane can do with his Huns, Faust knows he can do with his doubt: startle people up in terror, make existence sway under their feet, split people apart, make the cry of anxiety sound everywhere. And if he does it, he is still no Tamerlane; in a certain sense he is authorized — he has thought’s authorization. But Faust is a sympathetic nature. He loves existence; his soul knows no envy; he sees that he cannot stop the frenzy he may well be able to arouse; he craves no Herostratic fame. He keeps silent. He hides the doubt in his soul more carefully than a girl hides the fruit of a sinful love beneath her heart. He tries as well as he can to walk in step with other people; but what goes on inside him he consumes within himself, and in this way he offers himself as a sacrifice for the universal.

Now and then one can hear people complain, when some eccentric head stirs up a whirlwind of doubt; then they say: “If only he had kept silent!” Faust makes this idea real. Whoever has a notion of what it means for a human being to live on spirit also knows what doubt’s hunger is, and that the doubter is as hungry for life’s daily bread as for the nourishment of spirit. Now, all the pain Faust suffers may be a pretty good argument that it is not pride that has possessed him. Even so, I will use a little precaution, which I can easily invent. For just as Gregory of Rimini was called tortor infantium — torturer of infants — because he held that little children are damned, so I could be tempted to call myself tortor heroum — torturer of heroes; for I am most inventive where tormenting heroes is concerned. Faust sees Margaret — not after he has chosen pleasure, for my Faust does not choose pleasure at all. He does not see Margaret in Mephistopheles’s concave mirror; he sees her in all her lovable innocence. And since his soul has kept its love for people, he is also quite capable of falling in love with her. But he is a doubter; his doubt has annihilated actuality for him. For my Faust is so ideal that he does not belong among those scholarly doubters who doubt for one hour each semester from the lectern but otherwise can do everything else — just as they do the doubting too — without being in a state of spirit or acting by virtue of spirit. He is a doubter, and the doubter is as hungry for joy’s daily bread as for the food of spirit. Still, he stays true to his resolve and keeps silent: he speaks to no one about his doubt, and to Margaret not about his love either.

Naturally, Faust is too ideal a figure to rest content with the chatter that if he spoke he would set off a general discussion, or the whole thing would pass off without consequences, or perhaps, or perhaps. (Here, as any poet will easily see, the comic slumbers in the design: Faust could be brought into an ironic relation to those low-comic clowns who in our time run after doubt — who produce an outward argument that they really have doubted, a doctor’s certificate, for example; or swear they have doubted everything; or prove it by having met a doubter on their travels. These express messengers and sprinters in the world of spirit pick up, in the greatest haste, a little whiff of doubt from one person and of faith from another, and then wirthschaften — do their business — as best they can, according to whether the congregation wants fine sand or coarse sand.) Faust is too ideal a figure to shuffle around in slippers. Whoever does not have an infinite passion is not ideal; and whoever has an infinite passion has long since saved his soul out of such drivel. He keeps silent in order to sacrifice himself — or he speaks, conscious that he will throw everything into confusion.

If he keeps silent, ethics condemns him. For it says: “You shall acknowledge the universal, and it is precisely by speaking that you acknowledge it; and you may not have pity on the universal.” This consideration ought not to be forgotten when one sometimes judges a doubter harshly because he speaks. I am not inclined to judge such conduct leniently; but here, as everywhere, what matters is that the movements happen as the norm requires. If it comes to the worst, a doubter — even if by speaking he brought every possible misfortune on the world — is still far preferable to these miserable sweet-tooths who taste a little of everything, who want to cure doubt without knowing it, and who are therefore, as a rule, the immediate occasion for doubt’s breaking out wildly and uncontrollably. — If he speaks, he throws everything into confusion. For only afterward does he learn whether the confusion comes about or not; and the outcome cannot help a person — neither in the moment of action nor as regards the responsibility.

If he keeps silent on his own responsibility, he may well act magnanimously; but on top of his other pain he will feel a small spiritual trial. For the universal will keep tormenting him, saying: “You ought to have spoken. How will you ever be certain that it was not a hidden arrogance, after all, that guided your decision?”

If, on the other hand, the doubter can become the single individual who as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute, then his silence can receive an authorization. In that case he must turn his doubt into guilt. In that case he is in the paradox; but in that case his doubt is healed, even though he may come to have a different doubt.

Such a silence would be acknowledged even by the New Testament. Indeed, the New Testament even contains passages that commend irony, provided only that it is used to hide what is better. This movement, however, belongs to irony just as much as to any other movement whose ground is that subjectivity is higher than actuality. Our age wants to know nothing of this. In general it wants to know no more about irony than what Hegel has said — and he, strangely enough, did not understand much about it and bore a grudge against it, a grudge our age has good reasons not to give up, for it had better simply beware of irony. The Sermon on the Mount says: “When you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that people will not see that you are fasting.” This passage testifies outright that subjectivity is incommensurable with actuality — indeed, that it is permitted to deceive. If only the people who in our time flit about with loose talk of the idea of the congregation would read the New Testament, they might perhaps come to think otherwise.

But now Abraham — how did he act? For I have not forgotten, and the reader may now perhaps be good enough to remember, that it was in order to run up against this point that I entered into the whole preceding investigation. It was not so that Abraham would thereby become more understandable, but so that his incomprehensibility might become more disjointed. For, as I have said, Abraham I cannot understand; him I can only admire. It was also remarked that none of the stages described contained an analogy to Abraham. They were developed only so that, shown within their own sphere, each might, at the moment it deviated like a compass needle, point as it were to the boundary of the unknown land. Insofar as there could be any question of an analogy, it would have to be the paradox of sin. But that in turn lies in another sphere; it cannot explain Abraham, and is itself far easier to explain than Abraham.
So Abraham did not speak. He did not speak to Sarah, not to Eliezer, not to Isaac; he passed over the three ethical authorities. For the ethical had no higher expression for Abraham than family life.

Aesthetics permitted — indeed, demanded — silence of the single individual when by keeping silent he could save another. This alone is enough to show that Abraham does not fall within the range of aesthetics. His silence is by no means meant to save Isaac — just as, in general, his whole task, to sacrifice Isaac for his own sake and for God’s sake, is an offense to aesthetics. For aesthetics can certainly understand my sacrificing myself, but not my sacrificing someone else for my own sake. The aesthetic hero was silent. Ethics, however, condemned him, because he was silent by virtue of his accidental particularity. What determined him to keep silent was what he, as a human being, knew beforehand. This ethics cannot forgive: any such human knowledge is only an illusion. Ethics demands an infinite movement; it demands disclosure. So the aesthetic hero can speak, but will not.
